title: Temporal Proteomic Remodeling of Cerebral Arteries in Hypertensive Rats Reveals Progressive Vascular Changes Linked to Brain Diseases
projectDescription: Hypertension is a significant risk factor for several brain diseases, including stroke and dementia, yet the molecular mechanisms conferring to these risks remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated temporal proteomic remodeling of the cerebrovasculature in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs) and normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY) controls at 30 and 40 weeks of age, representing the effect of untreated hypertension from early adulthood to midlife.  Using discovery-based proteomics, RNA-sequencing data and comparison to previously published data, we have demonstrated a significant age-dependent change in the protein composition of the cerebrovasculature in the SHR model, which is partly mediated via the serum response factor (SRF) regulon. We identified a transient upregulation of mitotic (M-phase) proteins at 30 weeks, indicative of maladaptive smooth muscle proliferation. By 40 weeks, the expression of these proteins was normalized; however, extracellular matrix (ECM)-associated proteins diverged substantially. The ECM remodeling was supported by increased media-to-lumen ratio and collagen deposition from histological analysis.  Our findings reveal a novel temporal window during which hypertension drives a progressive remodeling of the cerebrovasculature. Collectively, the data supports a critical intervention window in early to midlife hypertension to prevent a molecular profile with brain disease-linked features.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cerebral arteries were homogenized in 100 μL of ice-cold lysis buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 8.5; 5 mM EDTA, pH 8.0; 150 mM NaCl; 10 mM KCl; 1% NP-40; and 1× complete protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche)) using three cycles of disruption with dissection scissors and processing with a handheld homogenizer. The resulting homogenates were centrifuged at 11,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected. Protein concentrations were measured using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific).  Homogenized artery extracts (50µg protein) were mixed with digestion buffer containing 0.5% sodium deoxycholate in 50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate, followed by heat treatment at 70 °C for 10 minutes. The samples were then cooled on ice and processed using filter-aided sample preparation (FASP) with flat spin filters (Microcon, 10 kDa cutoff). Proteins were reduced and alkylated in digestion buffer containing tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP, 0.5 M, 1:50 v/v; Sigma) and 2-chloroacetamide (0.5 M, 1:10 v/v; Sigma) for 30 minutes at 37 °C. Digestion was performed overnight at 37 °C using 0.5 μg of Trypsin/LysC mix (Promega) in digestion buffer. Centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 15 minutes was performed between each processing step. Peptide were desalted using stage-tips packed with styrene-divinylbenzene reversed-phase sulfonate (SDB-RPS) material (Affinisep, Lot: PP15B6). In brief, peptides were mixed with five volumes of 99% isopropanol (Sigma)/1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA, Sigma) and loaded onto the stage-tips, followed by centrifugation at 1,500 × g at 4 °C. The filters were washed twice in 99% isopropanol/1% TFA followed by 0.2% TFA. Peptides were eluted with 80% acetonitrile (Sigma)/2% ammonia (25%, Sigma), vacuum-dried, and resuspended in 2% acetonitrile/0.1% TFA prior to analysis.
dataProcessingProtocol: Peptides (1 µl injection) were analyzed on a Bruker TimsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) operated in positive ion mode. The mass spectrometer was coupled to a Dionex Ultimate 3000RSnano chromatography system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptide separation was performed on an Aurora C18 column (15 cm length, 75 μm inner diameter, 1.6 μm particles; IonOpticks) with a captive spray insert, and temperature was maintained at 50 °C. A solvent gradient of buffer A (0.1 % formic acid) and buffer B (99.9% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid) over 28 min, at a flow rate of 400 nl/min was used. The mass spectrometer was operated in data-independent acquisition (DIA) PASEF mode with a cycle time of 1.16 s. Raw DIA files were processed using DIA-NN software (v1.8.1) (https://github.com/vdemichev/diann) (Demichev et al. 2020). The UniProt FASTA Rattus norvegicus database (UP000002494_10116.fasta, containing 21,587 entries, and UP000002494_10116_additional.fasta, containing 9,981 entries; both from August 2020) was used. In DIA-NN, the options "FASTA digest for library-free search/library generation" and "Deep learning-based spectra, RTs, and IMs prediction" were enabled, while all other settings were left at default.
